newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain demands fair deal on joining EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain demands fair deal on joining EMU.

text.p: Madrid warned its European partners on Monday that if they overlook French shortcomings to let Paris join a single currency, it will expect the same treatment.

Just hours before the start of a two-day Franco-Spanish summit, Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told journalists Spain's economic health must be judged by the same yardstick as France's when the selection is made for joining the euro.

"Obviously there will be no difference between France and Spain," Matutes told journalists when asked whether Spain would require similar treatment in those cases where allowances were made for France not meeting economic criteria strictly.

Spain's six-month-old conservative government, which ousted the Socialists this spring after 13 years in power, has turned the nation's once quixotic European aspirations into what many economists see as a feasible option with an austere 1997 budget.
Meanwhile, France -- long considered an obligatory founder member of a successful currency launch -- has struggled to whip its finances into shape for the euro's scheduled 1999 debut.

As a result, suspicion is growing that France might be whisked into the founding group with a swish of political licence -- even if it cannot quite meet the criteria on deficit, debt, inflation, currency, and long-term interest rates.

Last week, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp reinforced these worries, saying the Maastricht treaty did not require nations to meet reference values exactly and that there was room for interpretation on the criteria set out in the document.

But analysts believe any leeway would be extended to France and not to Spain. They fear that the European currency core of Germany, its satellites and France sense an unpleasant odour to Spain's hurried fiscal clean-up.
"The priority for Germany (with respect to EMU) is France. For Europe, we are the spare wheel," said Alvaro Martinez, director of fixed income at AB Asesores last Thursday.
"From the fiscal point of view, Spain won't be any worse off than France," he added.

In an interview with Reuters last month, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said France and Germany must participate in the Euro launch but that the "Club Med" nations cannot join on the first round if the goal is to launch a currency as stable as the mark this century.
But Matutes made explicit what analysts had long suspected -- that Spain expects its sweat and toil in getting into economic shape to earn it the same advantages others have.
"All the countries that enter EMU are going to be in the same condition, with the same rights and the same obligations," Matutes said.
